lessons.title: Water Requirements at Different Growth Stages
lessons.body:
Cabbage needs different amounts of water at each stage of growth. From planting to harvest, the crop takes about 60 to 90 days, depending on the variety and climate. In the first two weeks after transplanting, the seedlings are small and have shallow roots. They need light, frequent watering to keep the top 15 cm of soil moist. In dry African conditions, this means watering every day or every other day, using about 2 to 3 liters per plant per week. A simple way to check is to stick your finger into the soil up to the second knuckle. If it feels dry, water.

From week 3 to week 6, cabbage plants grow fast. They form new leaves and start to build the head. Water needs increase to about 4 to 5 liters per plant per week. The roots go deeper, so you can water less often but more deeply. In sandy soils, water every 2 to 3 days. In clay soils, every 4 to 5 days. If you are in a hot, dry area like the Sahel, add 20 to 30 percent more water. A 20-liter bucket can water about 4 to 5 plants at this stage.

From week 7 until harvest, the cabbage heads fill out and become firm. This is the most critical stage for water. Lack of water now causes small, loose heads that crack easily. Give about 5 to 6 liters per plant per week. Keep the soil evenly moist, but never waterlogged. Too much water at this stage can split the heads. In rainy areas, you may not need to irrigate at all, but check the soil. If the top 10 cm is dry, give a little water.

A good rule for African smallholders: cabbage uses about 25 to 40 mm of water per week (1 mm = 1 liter per square meter). So for a 10 square meter bed, that is 250 to 400 liters per week. Adjust based on rainfall, temperature, and soil type. Mulching with dry grass or crop residues helps keep moisture in the soil and reduces how often you water.

lessons.title: Drip Irrigation Systems for Cabbage
lessons.body:
Drip irrigation is the most efficient way to water cabbage. It saves water because it delivers water directly to the plant roots, drop by drop, instead of wetting the whole field. For African farmers, drip systems can be low-cost and easy to set up. You need a water source (a tank, a well, or a tap), a main line (16 mm or 20 mm black polyethylene pipe), drip lines (12 mm or 16 mm with emitters spaced 30 cm apart), and connectors. A simple gravity system using a 200-liter drum raised 1 meter above the ground works well for a small plot.

To set up drip for cabbage, first prepare your beds. Space plants 40 cm apart in rows 60 cm apart. Lay one drip line per row of cabbage, with emitters near each plant. If your drip line has emitters every 30 cm, that is fine. Connect the drip lines to the main line using barbed connectors and a end cap. Flush the system before planting to remove dirt. Run the system for 30 to 60 minutes per day, depending on the weather. In hot weather, you may need two short sessions: one early morning, one late afternoon.

Drip irrigation has many benefits. It reduces water use by 30 to 50 percent compared to sprinklers. It also reduces weeds because only the crop row gets water. It keeps the leaves dry, which lowers the chance of fungal diseases like downy mildew. And it can be used with soluble fertilizers (fertigation), saving time and labor. However, drip systems need clean water. If your water has sand or debris, use a filter (a simple screen filter costs little). Also, drip lines can be damaged by rodents or farm tools, so handle them carefully.

For a 10 m x 10 m plot (100 square meters), you need about 10 drip lines of 10 meters each, plus a main line and connectors. The cost can be as low as $30 to $50 if you buy locally made drip tape. In many African countries, drip kits are available from agro-dealers or NGOs. After harvest, roll up the drip lines and store them in a cool, dark place. They can last 3 to 5 seasons if well cared for.

lessons.title: Sprinkler and Furrow Irrigation Methods
lessons.body:
Sprinkler irrigation sprays water into the air like rain. It is good for cabbage because it covers a large area quickly. You can use a simple bucket sprinkler (a plastic bucket with small holes punched in the bottom) or a knapsack sprayer with the nozzle removed. For larger plots, a small petrol or solar pump with a hose and sprinkler head works well. Space sprinklers so that water reaches all plants evenly. A common spacing is 12 m x 12 m for a rotating sprinkler. Run the system for 30 to 45 minutes, then check how deep the water went. Push a stick into the soil: if it is wet 15 cm deep, that is enough.

Sprinklers are easy to move and can be used on uneven land. But they wet the leaves, which can encourage diseases like black rot and downy mildew. To reduce this, water early in the morning so leaves dry during the day. Also, sprinklers lose water to evaporation, especially in hot, windy conditions. In dry areas, you may lose 20 to 30 percent of the water. So sprinklers are best for cooler, humid areas or when you have plenty of water.

Furrow irrigation is the oldest method. You make small channels (furrows) between rows of cabbage and let water flow into them. Water seeps into the soil and reaches the roots. Furrows work well on flat or gently sloping land with clay or loam soil. Space furrows 60 to 90 cm apart, and make them 10 to 15 cm deep. Water flows from a head ditch or a pipe. You can use a hose to fill each furrow, or let water run from a higher point. The water should reach the end of the furrow in 10 to 15 minutes. Do not let water stand in the furrow for more than 2 hours, or you may waterlog the soil.

Furrow irrigation is cheap and does not need special tools. But it uses more water than drip or sprinkler, and it can cause soil erosion if the slope is too steep. It also wets the whole field, so weeds grow everywhere. For cabbage, furrows are best in areas with heavy soil and limited access to pipes or pumps. Always check that water does not overflow and wash away soil. After watering, break the crust on the soil surface with a hoe to help air reach the roots.

lessons.title: Scheduling Irrigation Based on Soil Moisture
lessons.body:
Scheduling irrigation means deciding when and how much to water. The best way is to check soil moisture, not just look at the plants. Plants show wilting only after they are already stressed. A simple tool is a soil moisture meter. You can buy one for $10 to $20 from agro-dealers. Push the probe 15 cm into the soil near the roots. The meter reads from 1 (dry) to 10 (wet). For cabbage, keep the reading between 5 and 7. If it drops below 4, water immediately. If it stays above 8, stop watering until it drops.

If you cannot afford a meter, use the feel method. Take a handful of soil from 15 cm deep. Squeeze it in your hand. If it forms a ball that holds together but breaks easily when you poke it, the moisture is good. If it crumbles and falls apart, it is too dry. If it drips water, it is too wet. Do this test every morning in different parts of your plot. Also, dig a small hole with a hoe to see how deep the moisture goes. Cabbage roots go 30 to 45 cm deep, so you want moisture at least 20 cm down.

Another method is to use a tensiometer. This is a tube filled with water and a gauge that measures how hard plants have to pull to get water. For cabbage, irrigate when the tensiometer reads -30 to -40 centibars (cb). At -60 cb, the crop is stressed. Tensiometers cost more ($50 to $100) but are very accurate. They are best for commercial growers. For most smallholders, the feel method or a moisture meter is enough.

You can also schedule by days. In hot, dry weather, water every 2 to 3 days. In cool, cloudy weather, every 4 to 5 days. But always check the soil first. Overwatering wastes water and leaches nutrients. Underwatering reduces yield. A good rule: cabbage needs about 25 to 40 mm of water per week. If you get 10 mm of rain, you only need to add 15 to 30 mm. Use a simple rain gauge (a straight-sided tin can) to measure rainfall. Keep a record of when you water and how much rain you get. This helps you plan better next season.

lessons.title: Managing Waterlogging and Drainage
lessons.body:
Waterlogging happens when the soil is full of water and air cannot reach the roots. Cabbage is very sensitive to waterlogging. If the roots sit in water for more than 24 to 48 hours, they stop growing, turn brown, and rot. The plant wilts even though the soil is wet. You may also see yellow leaves and stunted heads. In Africa, waterlogging is common in low-lying areas, during heavy rains, or when you over-irrigate. The first sign is standing water on the surface. If you see this, act fast.

To prevent waterlogging, make raised beds. Raise the soil 20 to 30 cm high and 1 meter wide. This keeps the roots above the water table. In flat areas, dig drainage furrows around the plot. Make them 30 cm deep and 30 cm wide. Connect them to a lower point so water can flow away. If your plot is on a slope, dig contour drains across the slope to slow water down. For small gardens, you can also plant cabbage on ridges. Space ridges 60 cm apart and plant on top.

If waterlogging already happened, stop watering immediately. Dig small channels to let water drain. Do not walk on the wet soil, as this compacts it and makes things worse. Once the water is gone, let the soil dry for a few days. Then loosen the top 10 cm with a fork or hoe to let air in. If the plants are still alive, they may recover. But if the roots are brown and mushy, remove those plants and replant if there is time. To avoid future problems, add organic matter like compost or manure. It improves soil structure and helps water drain faster.

In areas with heavy clay soil, mix in sand or rice husks to improve drainage. Also, choose cabbage varieties that tolerate wet conditions, such as 'Copenhagen Market' or 'Golden Acre'. But no variety survives long in standing water. So drainage is key. Check your field after every heavy rain. If water stands for more than a few hours, fix the drainage before the next rain. A simple spade and a little labor can save your crop.

lessons.title: Water Conservation Practices in Cabbage Farming
lessons.body:
Water is scarce in many parts of Africa, so conserving it is essential. The first practice is mulching. Spread a 5 to 10 cm layer of dry grass, straw, or crop residues around your cabbage plants. Mulch reduces evaporation from the soil by up to 70 percent. It also keeps the soil cool and suppresses weeds. Do not use fresh grass or hay that contains seeds, as it may bring weeds. Apply mulch after transplanting when the plants are about 15 cm tall. Reapply as it breaks down.

Second, water early in the morning or late in the evening. Midday watering loses a lot to evaporation. Early morning is best because leaves dry quickly, reducing disease. Also, water deeply and less often. This encourages roots to grow deeper, making plants more drought-tolerant. A deep watering every 3 to 4 days is better than a light watering every day. For drip irrigation, run the system for longer but less frequently.

Third, use greywater or rainwater. Greywater from washing dishes or clothes can be used on cabbage, but avoid water with soap or bleach. Rainwater harvesting is cheap and effective. Place drums or tanks under gutters to catch roof runoff. A 200-liter drum can collect water from a small roof during one storm. You can also dig small basins around plants to capture rain. In dry areas, use sunken beds (zai pits) that hold water.

Fourth, improve soil organic matter. Add compost, manure, or cover crops. Organic matter acts like a sponge, holding water in the soil for longer. A soil with 3 to 5 percent organic matter can hold twice as much water as sandy soil. You can make compost from kitchen scraps, crop residues, and animal manure. Apply 2 to 3 handfuls per plant at planting. Also, practice crop rotation with deep-rooted crops like maize or beans, which improve soil structure.

Finally, control weeds. Weeds compete with cabbage for water. Remove them by hand or with a hoe. A weedy field can lose 30 to 50 percent of its water to weeds. Mulching also helps control weeds. And fix leaks in your irrigation system. A dripping pipe or a broken sprinkler can waste hundreds of liters per day. Check your system weekly and repair any leaks immediately. By combining these practices, you can grow healthy cabbage with less water.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Water and Irrigation Management for Cabbage

Cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. capitata) is one of the most widely grown brassicas in sub-Saharan Africa, from the highlands of Kenya and Ethiopia to the cooler zones of South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Cameroon. It is a shallow-rooted, moisture-sensitive crop: the bulk of its feeder roots sit in the top 20â30 cm of soil, so both under- and over-watering translate directly into lost marketable heads and lost income. For a commercial grower, irrigation is not a "cost centre" â it is the single input that most reliably determines head weight, uniformity, and the ability to hit contract volumes. This reference lesson consolidates the practical numbers, systems, and scheduling rules you need to run cabbage irrigation as a business decision.

1. Water Requirements at Different Growth Stages

Cabbage water use is usually expressed as crop evapotranspiration (ETc), calculated as ETc = ETo Ã Kc, where ETo is reference evapotranspiration (from a weather station or FAO estimates) and Kc is the crop coefficient for that growth stage. Total seasonal requirement for a 90â120 day crop is typically 350â500 mm, but the critical point is when that water is applied. Moisture stress during head formation causes small, loose, or split heads â the stage where irrigation failure is most expensive.

Table 1: Indicative cabbage water use by growth stage (90â110 day crop)
Growth stage Days after transplant Kc Daily ETc (mm/day)* Business implication
Establishment 0â20 0.5 2â3 Light, frequent watering to root transplants; avoid waterlogging
Vegetative development 21â45 0.8 3â5 Build leaf area; nitrogen uptake peaks
Head formation (critical) 46â75 1.05 5â7 Stress here = small/split heads; never let soil dry below 60% field capacity
Maturity / harvest 76â110 0.9 4â6 Reduce irrigation 7â10 days before harvest to limit splitting and improve storage life

*ETc assumes ETo of 4â6 mm/day, typical of highland and cool-season production zones. Source: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Allen et al., 1998); values interpreted for African smallholder and commercial conditions.

2. Drip Irrigation Systems for Cabbage

Drip (trickle) irrigation is the highest-efficiency option for cabbage, achieving 85â95% water application efficiency compared with 50â70% for furrow. For a commercial operation, the business case is straightforward: drip reduces water pumping costs, cuts weed pressure between rows, allows fertigation (injecting soluble fertiliser directly into the root zone), and keeps foliage dry, which lowers disease pressure from black rot and downy mildew.

Practical layout for cabbage: use 16 mm lateral lines with in-line emitters at 30 cm spacing and 1â2 L/h discharge, laid one line per cabbage row or one line per two rows on 60â75 cm beds. Operating pressure is typically 1.0â1.5 bar. Run times are short â often 30â60 minutes per cycle â so a single system can irrigate multiple blocks in one day. On smallholder plots in Kenya, Ethiopia, and Tanzania, low-cost drip kits (gravity-fed from a raised tank or drum) are increasingly common and pay back within one to two seasons on cabbage alone.

Maintenance is the failure point. Emitter clogging from silt, algae, and iron is the leading cause of under-irrigation in African drip systems. Budget for filtration (screen or disc filters, 120â150 mesh), flush the laterals monthly, and chlorinate or acidify once per season where water quality demands it.

3. Sprinkler and Furrow Irrigation Methods

Sprinkler systems (hand-move, drag-hose, or solid-set) suit cabbage well because the crop tolerates overhead water and the canopy is relatively upright. Efficiency is 70â85%. The main drawbacks are higher evaporation losses in hot, windy conditions, and increased foliar disease risk if irrigation is applied late in the day. In South Africa and Zimbabwe, solid-set sprinklers are common on commercial cabbage blocks; in East Africa, hand-move sprinklers dominate on medium-scale farms.

Furrow irrigation remains the cheapest method to install and is still widely used on alluvial soils along river valleys. Efficiency is low (50â70%) and it demands accurate land levelling. Cabbage is often planted on ridges between furrows so water moves laterally to the roots. The critical management rule is to never let water stand against the stem for more than a few hours, as this promotes stem rot and root asphyxiation.

Table 2: Comparison of irrigation methods for cabbage production
Method Water efficiency Capital cost Labour Best fit in Africa
Drip 85â95% High Low Commercial blocks, water-scarce areas, fertigation programmes
Sprinkler 70â85% Medium Medium Mediumâlarge farms with reliable water and power
Furrow 50â70% Low High Smallholders on levelled soils near rivers or canals
Manual (watering can) 40â60% Very low Very high Nursery and very small plots only

Source: FAO Land and Water Division, Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Methods (Training Manual No. 5); efficiency ranges corroborated by AQUASTAT country data for sub-Saharan Africa.

4. Scheduling Irrigation Based on Soil Moisture

Scheduling by calendar alone wastes water and money. The professional approach is to irrigate when soil moisture in the root zone drops to a defined trigger point â typically 50â60% of field capacity for cabbage, and no lower than 60% during head formation. Three practical tools are used across Africa:

  • Tensiometers placed at 15 cm and 30 cm depth. Irrigate when readings reach â30 to â40 kPa (cabbage is a relatively "thirsty" crop).
  • Gravimetric sampling â oven-drying soil samples. Accurate but slow; best for calibration.
  • The "feel and appearance" method â a free, field-ready technique taught by extension services. Squeeze a handful of soil from 15 cm depth: if it forms a weak ball that breaks easily, it is time to irrigate.

For growers with smartphone access, FAO's ETo calculator and national weather service data (e.g. Kenya Meteorological Department, SAWS in South Africa) allow a simple water-balance schedule: subtract daily ETc from rainfall and irrigation, and irrigate when the deficit reaches the allowable depletion for that growth stage.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Waterlogging, Disease and Agro-chemical Risk

Cabbage is highly susceptible to black rot (Xanthomonas campestris) and clubroot in waterlogged, poorly drained soils. Never irrigate to the point where standing water remains in the root zone for more than 4â6 hours. If you apply agro-chemicals through a drip or sprinkler system (chemigation), install a double check valve and an air gap to prevent backflow contamination of the water source â this is a legal requirement in most African countries and a serious public health risk. Always wear PPE when handling chlorine, acid, or fertiliser injectants, and never mix them in enclosed spaces.

5. Managing Waterlogging and Drainage

In high-rainfall highland zones (e.g. Kenya's Aberdare ranges, Ethiopia's Amhara highlands, Cameroon's western highlands), waterlogging is a bigger yield threat than drought. Cabbage roots need oxygen; 24â48 hours of saturation can cause permanent root damage and open the door to root rots. Practical drainage measures:

  • Plant on raised beds or ridges 20â30 cm high â the single most effective drainage intervention.
  • Cut open drains at the bottom of the slope and between blocks to move excess water off the field.
  • Use subsoiling once per season where a plough pan restricts downward water movement.
  • Add organic matter (compost, manure) to improve soil structure and infiltration.
  • Where soils are heavy clay, consider tile or mole drainage on commercial blocks.

6. Water Conservation Practices in Cabbage Farming

Water is increasingly the binding constraint on African vegetable production, and conservation is a direct profitability lever. Priority practices:

  • Mulching with straw, grass, or plastic film reduces evaporation by 30â50% and suppresses weeds.
  • Organic matter and compost increase the soil's water-holding capacity â every 1% increase in soil organic carbon can raise available water capacity significantly.
  • Deficit irrigation at non-critical stages (establishment and late maturity) saves water without reducing head weight, provided the head-formation stage is fully supplied.
  • Rainwater harvesting â roof catchment, lined ponds, and check dams â is standard practice on successful commercial cabbage farms in Kenya and South Africa.
  • Solar-powered pumping is rapidly replacing diesel in off-grid areas, cutting both cost and carbon footprint.
  • Regular maintenance of pumps, filters, and pipes â leaks and clogged emitters can waste 20â30% of applied water.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Calculate ETc = ETo Ã Kc weekly; never irrigate by habit alone.
  2. Keep soil moisture above 60% of field capacity during head formation â this is the make-or-break stage.
  3. Stop irrigation 7â10 days before harvest to reduce splitting and extend shelf life.
  4. Check drip emitters and filters monthly; flush laterals and clean filters.
  5. Use tensiometers or the feel method at 15 cm and 30 cm depth to trigger irrigation.
  6. Plant on raised beds in high-rainfall zones; maintain open drains year-round.
  7. Mulch to cut evaporation and weed pressure â a low-cost, high-return practice.
  8. Install backflow prevention if using chemigation; wear PPE when handling injectants.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56: Crop Evapotranspiration (Kc values and ETc calculation).
  • FAO â Irrigation Water Management: Irrigation Methods (Training Manual No. 5).
  • FAO AQUASTAT â Country water and irrigation data for Africa.
  • International Water Management Institute (IWMI) â Research and tools on smallholder irrigation in Africa.
  • Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) â Crop and irrigation advisory materials.

Business takeaway: In cabbage, irrigation is a margin decision, not a technical afterthought. Every millimetre applied at the wrong stage is money lost; every millimetre saved through drip, mulch, or good scheduling is money earned. Get the head-formation window right, keep the system maintained, and manage drainage as carefully as you manage water supply â that is what separates profitable cabbage growers from the rest.

quiz.q: How much water does a cabbage plant need per week during the first two weeks after transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Young seedlings need about 2-3 liters per plant per week to keep the topsoil moist.

quiz.q: Which growth stage is most critical for water in cabbage?
quiz.explanation: During head formation, lack of water causes small, loose heads and cracking.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to check if cabbage needs water?
options: A) Look at the leaves for wilting
B) Stick your finger into the soil
quiz.explanation: Checking soil moisture by feel is a reliable, low-cost method.

quiz.q: In hot, dry areas, how much more water should you add for cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Hot, dry conditions increase evaporation, so add 20-30% more water.

quiz.q: How much water does a 10 square meter cabbage bed need per week?
quiz.explanation: Cabbage uses 25-40 mm per week, which equals 250-400 liters for 10 square meters.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of drip irrigation for cabbage?
options: A) It is the cheapest method
B) It saves water and reduces weeds
D) It works without a water source
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to roots, saving water and reducing weed growth.

quiz.q: What spacing of emitters is recommended for drip lines in cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Emitters spaced 30 cm apart are suitable for cabbage planted 40 cm apart.

quiz.q: How long should you run a drip system for cabbage in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: In hot weather, run the system for 30-60 minutes, possibly twice a day.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of drip irrigation regarding plant diseases?
quiz.explanation: Drip irrigation keeps leaves dry, reducing fungal diseases like downy mildew.

quiz.q: What is a common problem with drip systems if water is not clean?
quiz.explanation: Dirty water can clog emitters, so a filter is needed.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of sprinkler irrigation for cabbage?
options: B) It wets leaves and encourages disease
C) It cannot cover large areas
quiz.explanation: Sprinklers wet the leaves, which can promote fungal and bacterial diseases.

quiz.q: When is the best time to use sprinklers to reduce disease?
quiz.explanation: Early morning watering allows leaves to dry during the day, reducing disease risk.

quiz.q: How deep should furrows be for cabbage irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Furrows 10-15 cm deep allow water to flow and seep into the root zone.

quiz.q: What is a major disadvantage of furrow irrigation?
options: A) It uses more water and causes erosion
D) It cannot be used on clay soil
quiz.explanation: Furrow irrigation uses more water and can cause soil erosion on slopes.

quiz.q: How long should water run in a furrow to avoid waterlogging?
quiz.explanation: Do not let water stand in furrows for more than 2 hours to prevent waterlogging.

quiz.q: What is the ideal soil moisture meter reading for cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Keep the meter reading between 5 and 7 for optimal cabbage growth.

quiz.q: What does it mean if a handful of soil from 15 cm deep drips water when squeezed?
options: D) Soil needs more organic matter
quiz.explanation: Dripping water indicates the soil is waterlogged and needs drainage.

quiz.q: At what tensiometer reading should you irrigate cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Irrigate when tensiometer reads -30 to -40 cb to avoid crop stress.

quiz.q: How often should you water cabbage in cool, cloudy weather?
quiz.explanation: In cool weather, water every 4-5 days, but always check soil moisture.

quiz.q: What is a simple rain gauge made from?
quiz.explanation: A straight-sided tin can is a simple rain gauge to measure rainfall.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of waterlogging in cabbage?
options: C) Standing water on the surface
quiz.explanation: Standing water on the surface is the first visible sign of waterlogging.

quiz.q: How high should raised beds be to prevent waterlogging?
quiz.explanation: Raised beds 20-30 cm high keep roots above the water table.

quiz.q: What should you do immediately if waterlogging occurs?
options: B) Stop watering and dig drainage channels
quiz.explanation: Stop watering and dig channels to drain excess water quickly.

quiz.q: How can organic matter help with waterlogging?
options: A) It makes soil hold more water
quiz.explanation: Organic matter improves soil structure and helps water drain faster.

quiz.q: Which cabbage variety tolerates wet conditions better?
quiz.explanation: Copenhagen Market is known to tolerate wet conditions better than some others.

quiz.q: How does mulching help conserve water?
options: B) It reduces evaporation by up to 70%
quiz.explanation: Mulch reduces evaporation from the soil surface by up to 70%.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to water cabbage to conserve water?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Watering early morning or late evening reduces evaporation losses.

quiz.q: Why is deep watering better than light watering?
quiz.explanation: Deep watering encourages roots to grow deeper, making plants more drought-tolerant.

quiz.q: What type of water should you avoid using on cabbage?
quiz.explanation: Greywater with soap or bleach can harm cabbage plants.

quiz.q: How can you capture rainwater for cabbage irrigation?
quiz.explanation: Placing drums under gutters captures roof runoff for irrigation.
